extracted.intended_audience: immigration attorneys, advocates, agency rulewriters, and members of the public interested in public charge rulemaking and related Federal Register proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: A Federal Register search-results/listing page aggregating Federal Register documents and excerpts that match the term 'public charge', including proposed and final rules, notices of information collection, and related agency guidance. The page is intended to help readers find rulemaking materials and notices relevant to public charge policy and associated administrative procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'public charge' for inadmissibility (DHS 2022 rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS would determine that a noncitizen is likely at any time to become a public charge if the noncitizen is likely at any time to become primarily dependent on the government for subsistence, as demonstrated by either the receipt of public cash assistance for income maintenance or long-term institutionalization at government expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation contrasts with other regulatory approaches (e.g., 2019 IFR). The excerpts note that the statute and case law do not prescribe a precise degree or type of assistance that makes someone a public charge, which informs DHS's interpretive choice. The rule implements a policy that focuses on primary dependence demonstrated by public cash assistance or long-term institutionalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions, waivers, and availability of public charge bonds
rubrics_metrics.description: Some categories of aliens are exempt from the public charge ground of inadmissibility, while others, if found inadmissible under the public charge ground, may apply for a waiver of the public charge ground of inadmissibility or submit a public charge bond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The excerpts emphasize that certain statutory exemptions exist and that DHS/USCIS may permit waivers or acceptance of a public charge bond in some cases. Guidance around who is exempt, eligibility for waivers, and bond procedures is set out in agency rule texts and related notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: USCIS Form I-945 (Public Charge Bond) collection requirement and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Title of the Form/Collection: Public Charge Bond (I-945). USCIS uses Form I-945 to ensure that the conditions of the bond are fully articulated and met when USCIS accepts the public charge bond posting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PRA notices explain the information collected, categories of respondents (primary: individuals or households), and estimated respondent burden and costs. The form exists because of the complexity of federal bond conditions; agencies solicit public comment on the collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions and criteria for cancellation of a public charge bond
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS may cancel a public charge bond at any time after determining that the alien is not likely at any time to become a public charge. A bond may also be cancelled to allow substitution of another bond. A public charge bond will be cancelled by USCIS upon review following the fifth anniversary, provided the alien did not breach such bond by receiving either public cash assistance for income maintenance or long-term institutionalization at government expense prior to death, permanent departure, or naturalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cancellation can occur on several grounds (reassessment of likelihood, substitution, time-based review). Breach events (receipt of public cash assistance or long-term institutionalization) can prevent cancellation. The notices provide procedural timing and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency roles and contexts for applying the public charge ground
rubrics_metrics.description: Three different agencies are responsible for applying the public charge ground of inadmissibility, each in a different context or contexts. DHS primarily applies the public charge ground of inadmissibility to applicants for admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The excerpts signal that different agencies (DHS, State Department, and others) apply the public charge ground in different administrative contexts (visas, admission, adjustment of status) and that regulatory texts and foreign affairs/manual guidance interact across agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence requirement for visa applicants (e.g., Diversity Visa) to show not likely to become a public charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Before being issued a visa you must demonstrate that you will not become a public charge in the United States. Applicants should familiarize themselves with the Department of State's guidance on how the likelihood of becoming a public charge is assessed and what evidence can be provided to demonstrate that you are not likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency procedural guidance (e.g., Diversity Visa instructions, FAM guidance) describes what kinds of documentary evidence or demonstrations are appropriate. Comment notices often point applicants to those guidance documents for examples of acceptable evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of administrative information (e.g., change-of-address data) to enforce public charge and benefit-receipt rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Change of address and other administrative collections will be used to enforce immigration laws, including the public charge ground of deportation under INA section 237(a)(5), and to identify aliens who may be receiving means-tested public benefits in violation of eligibility restrictions established by PRWORA (8 U.S.C. 1601 et seq.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRA notices and rule texts explain that data collected for one administrative purpose (like address updates) can be used to coordinate with benefit-granting agencies and to detect potential violations, and agencies solicit comment on privacy, burden, and coordination issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive approach: statutory ambiguity about degree/type of assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS has noted that 'the term public charge is ambiguous as to how much government assistance an individual must receive or the type of assistance an individual must receive to be considered a public charge. The statute and case law do not prescribe the degree to which an alien must be receiving public benefits to be considered a public charge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretive observation informs why agencies propose specific definitional tests (e.g., primary dependence by cash assistance or long-term institutionalization) and why different rulemakings have taken different approaches. It is cited in preambles to justify regulatory choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public participation and PRA notice elements for information collections related to public charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Information collection notices are published to obtain comments regarding the nature of the information collection, the categories of respondents, the estimated burden (time, effort, resources), the estimated cost to the respondent, and the actual information collection instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies publish PRA notices (e.g., reinstatement/changes with 30-day comment windows) to solicit public comment on forms like I-945 and I-864; the notices identify the title, agency form number, affected public, and abstract/purpose of the collection, and invite comment on privacy and burden concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy framing: self-reliance and benefits not to incentivize immigration
rubrics_metrics.description: Rescission proponents argue that restoring broader discretion to evaluate all pertinent facts would align with long-standing policy that aliens in the United States should be self-reliant and government benefits should not incentivize immigration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy rationale appears in preambles and proposed rescission documents as an evaluative standard shaping rulemaking choices (i.e., whether to adopt a narrower definition of public charge or restore broader case-by-case discretion).
